questiontext.text: What is the amortized cost of decrease-key in a Fibonacci heap?

feedback.text: Correct — this fast decrease-key is the Fibonacci heap's signature property.
No — decrease-key is O(1) amortized; extract-min is the O(log n) one.
No — it is O(1) amortized via cutting and cascading cuts.
No — the amortized bound is O(1).

generalfeedback.text: Decrease-key cuts the node from its parent (possibly triggering cascading cuts) in O(1) amortized time — the property that makes Fibonacci heaps attractive for Dijkstra and Prim.

questiontext.text: What is the amortized cost of extract-min in a Fibonacci heap?

feedback.text: Correct — extract-min consolidates the root list and is O(log n) amortized.
No — insert, find-min, decrease-key, and merge are O(1); extract-min is O(log n).
No — consolidation gives O(log n) amortized.
No — the amortized bound is O(log n).

generalfeedback.text: Extract-min removes the min root and then consolidates trees of equal degree, paying the deferred work; amortized this is O(log n).

questiontext.text: Using a Fibonacci heap as the priority queue, Dijkstra's algorithm runs in which time bound?

feedback.text: Correct — O(1) decrease-key across E edges plus O(log V) extract-min over V vertices.
That is the binary-heap bound; the Fibonacci heap improves it to O(E + V log V).
That is the simple array bound, not the Fibonacci-heap result.
No — the V extract-min operations still cost O(V log V) in total.

generalfeedback.text: The O(1) amortized decrease-key removes the log factor from the E relaxations, so Dijkstra (and Prim) reach O(E + V log V).

questiontext.text: Which mechanism does a Fibonacci heap rely on to achieve its bounds?

answer.text: Lazy consolidation of the root list plus cascading cuts using marked nodes

feedback.text: Correct — work is deferred until extract-min, and marks bound the damage from cuts.

answer.text: Rotations to keep every tree height-balanced

feedback.text: No — Fibonacci heaps do not rotate; they cut and consolidate lazily.

answer.text: Storing all keys in a single sorted array

feedback.text: No — it is a lazy forest of heap-ordered trees.
No — there is no hashing involved.

generalfeedback.text: Inserts and merges just splice into the root list (lazy); consolidation happens only at extract-min, and cascading cuts on marked nodes keep trees from degrading.

questiontext.text: In a Fibonacci heap, insert and merge each take O(1) amortized time.

feedback.text: Correct — both just splice into the root list, deferring real work to extract-min.
Both insert and merge are O(1) amortized; the deferred work is paid at extract-min.

questiontext.text: Despite excellent asymptotic bounds, Fibonacci heaps are often slower than simpler heaps in practice due to large constant factors.

feedback.text: Correct — bookkeeping overhead makes them lose to binary or pairing heaps on typical inputs.
It is true — their constant factors and pointer overhead often make them slower in real use.

questiontext.text: Cutting a node whose second child is lost, and possibly its parent in turn, is called a ______ cut. (one word)

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which operations run in O(1) amortized time in a Fibonacci heap? (select all that apply)

feedback.text: Yes — O(1) amortized, the heap's headline feature.
Yes — a pointer to the minimum root gives O(1).
No — extract-min is O(log n) amortized, not O(1).
No — arbitrary search is not a supported O(1) heap operation.

generalfeedback.text: Insert, find-min, decrease-key, and merge are O(1) amortized; extract-min is O(log n) amortized, and arbitrary search is not an efficient heap operation.
